question_text: If y = eᵃ ˢⁱⁿ⁻¹ˣ, prove that dy/dx = ay/√(1 − x²).

mark_split.label: Differentiate the exponential and name it y

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say why the answer can be written in terms of y, and what the exponent differentiates to.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Differentiate the exponential and name it y
steps.margin_note: First mark. eᵘ differentiates to eᵘ times du/dx, and here eᵘ is the whole of y. That is the reason the answer is stated in terms of y rather than the exponential.
steps.memory_tip: An exponential differentiates to itself, so eᵃ ˢⁱⁿ⁻¹ˣ can be replaced by y at any point in the working.
lines: Given y = eᵃ ˢⁱⁿ⁻¹ˣ, that is y = eᵘ where u = a Sin⁻¹x and a is a constant.
The exponential factor eᵃ ˢⁱⁿ⁻¹ˣ is y itself, so dy/dx = y · d/dx(a Sin⁻¹x)

recall.must_convey: That d/dx(eᵘ) = eᵘ·du/dx, and that the eᵘ factor is y itself, so dy/dx = y times the derivative of the exponent.
accept: e power u differentiates to e power u times du by dx
the exponential that comes back is y itself
replace e power a sin inverse x by y
e power u ne malli vasthundi, adi y ye
dy by dx is y times the derivative of the power

steps.why: The target has y on the right side, which only makes sense once the repeated exponential is recognised as y. Naming it here is what makes the last line match the statement being proved.
common_mistakes: Differentiating the exponential to a Sin⁻¹x · eᵃ ˢⁱⁿ⁻¹ˣ⁻¹, using the power rule.
Leaving the answer as an exponential and never connecting it back to y.

steps.label: Differentiate the exponent and finish
steps.margin_note: Second mark. a is a constant multiplier inside the exponent, so it stays as it is, and d/dx(Sin⁻¹x) = 1/√(1 − x²), valid for −1 < x < 1.
steps.memory_tip: Sin⁻¹ contributes 1/√(1 − x²). The constant a is unchanged and stays as a multiplier beside the y.
lines: d/dx(Sin⁻¹x) = 1/√(1 − x²),  so  d/dx(a Sin⁻¹x) = a/√(1 − x²)

recall.must_convey: That d/dx(a Sin⁻¹x) = a/√(1 − x²), so dy/dx = ay/√(1 − x²).
accept: sin inverse x differentiates to one over root one minus x squared
a stays outside so the exponent gives a over root one minus x squared
the answer is a y over root one minus x squared
sin inverse ki one by root one minus x square vasthundi
multiply y by a over root one minus x squared
heard_as: one by root one minus x squared

steps.why: The proof finishes because the exponential appears again unchanged and is replaced by y. Nothing is cancelled or rearranged, which is why this question is short even though it is written as a proof.
common_mistakes: Using 1/(1 + x²), which is the Tan⁻¹ derivative.
Dropping the constant a from the numerator.

insider_note: The exponential factor IS y, so replace it rather than writing it out again — that is what produces the y on the right-hand side. The a comes out of a Sin⁻¹x.
